article_title: Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators
citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators (CIRCLS/Digital Promise, 2024)
description: A bilingual reference glossary published on circls.org and shared on informalscience.org, written so that "educators to reference when learning about and using artificial intelligence (AI)". It opens with a definition of AI and then defines AI-related terms in alphabetical order, pairing each English entry with a Spanish translation. It was last updated March 31, 2024, and is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.
requirements: Intended as a reference for educators who are learning about and using AI; entries are alphabetical, starting from a base definition of AI.
constraints: The authors note it was last updated on March 31, 2024, so definitions reflect the field as of that date.
target_learning_goals: Understanding artificial intelligence terminology for educational practice
examples: Entries include Artificial Intelligence, Algorithm, ChatGPT, Computer Vision, Critical AI, Training Data, Foundation Models, Human-Centered Perspective, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Adaptive Learning, Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning, Machine Learning, Neural Networks, Robots, and UX/UI design.
key_sources: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/ed330bf1-6697-4cb7-9189-79eba8eb0a1e

article_title: AI literacy and scenario-based ethical judgment about generative AI among undergraduate students
citation: Reed, J. M., Ferdig, R. E., Dodson, T. M., Gunstad, J., & Hughes, J. W. (2026). AI Literacy and Scenario-based Ethical Judgment About Generative AI Among Undergraduate Students. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09757-w
title: Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test (GLAT) as an objective AI literacy measure
description: The GLAT (Jin et al., 2025) is "a 20-item multiple-choice performance assessment of demonstrated generative AI knowledge, skills, and ethical understanding", with domains covering Know & understand (8 items), Use & apply (3 items), Evaluate and create (4 items), and Ethics (5 items). Because the study outcome also assessed ethical judgment, the authors computed a 15-item Non-Ethics GLAT score (KR-20 = 0.65) for primary analyses to reduce criterion contamination; the full 20-item score showed KR-20 = 0.72.
requirements: Used with a 15-item Non-Ethics subscore when the outcome itself measures ethical judgment, to reduce conceptual overlap
constraints: Non-Ethics score showed modest internal consistency (KR-20 = 0.65)
Conceptual overlap between general AI literacy and ethical judgment may not have been eliminated completely
target_learning_goals: demonstrated generative AI knowledge, skills, and ethical understanding
examples: Each item includes one correct response and three distractors; total scores range from 0 to 20
key_sources: Reed, J. M., Ferdig, R. E., Dodson, T. M., Gunstad, J., & Hughes, J. W. (2026). AI Literacy and Scenario-based Ethical Judgment About Generative AI Among Undergraduate Students. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09757-w

article_title: The agency gap in AI-supported writing: how reactive and proactive agent designs shape multimodal reasoning
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Kaixun Yang, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2025). The Agency Gap in AI-Supported Writing: How Reactive and Proactive Agent Designs Shape Multimodal Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04398
title: Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test (GLAT), a 20-item performance-based instrument
description: The GLAT is a performance-based 20-item multiple-choice instrument measuring generative AI literacy across four dimensions: understanding, applying, creating with, and making ethical judgements about GenAI. Each item has four response options, and a corrected total score (with correction for guessing) served as a standardised continuous predictor in the study's regression and mediation models. It was chosen over self-report confidence scales because it assesses demonstrated knowledge relevant to prompting, evaluating, and using generative systems.
requirements: Requires the published correction-for-guessing formula for four-option items; the study relied on the instrument's published validation evidence rather than new factor validation
constraints: Published validation includes expert review and a 204-participant item-relevance study; the article notes its own modest sample precluded new factor validation
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: measuring demonstrated generative AI literacy including prompting and evaluative judgement
examples: Published validation evidence reports Cronbach's α = 0.76 and a stable two-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = 0.007)
key_sources: Yueqiao Jin, Kaixun Yang, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2025). The Agency Gap in AI-Supported Writing: How Reactive and Proactive Agent Designs Shape Multimodal Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04398

article_title: GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283
title: GLAT: a 20-item multiple-choice performance-based assessment of GenAI literacy for higher education
description: GLAT is a performance-based multiple-choice instrument designed to measure generative AI literacy among higher education students, targeting technical proficiency, ethical awareness, and critical evaluation of GenAI outputs. It was built through blueprint construction, item generation, expert review, and CTT-based item selection, yielding a final 20-item set. The article reports it as filling a gap in self-report-dominant AI literacy assessment.
requirements: Items must be developed and validated following established psychological and educational measurement procedures, including expert review and pilot testing
constraints: Developed and validated with higher education students recruited via Prolific; the article positions it for higher education contexts
target_learning_goals: generative AI literacy, including foundational knowledge, application, ethical awareness, and critical evaluation
examples: The initial 25-item version covered dimensions such as Know & Understand, Use & Apply, Evaluate & Create, and Ethics, with items like identifying what a token is in an LLM and how RAG enhances an LLM
key_sources: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283

article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Global–local switching paradigm as a measure of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style
description: The global–local switching paradigm is the behavioral task used in this study to assess cognitive control in high-school students. The article describes it as a task that "provides well-established measures of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style". Students in both the bilingual-education and regular-education groups performed the paradigm, and its switching costs and global precedence effect served as the outcome measures contrasting the two groups.
requirements: Administered to both comparison groups so switching costs and the global precedence effect can be contrasted between educational programs
target_learning_goals: Assessment of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style
examples: Two groups of Dutch high-school students, one taught in English and Dutch and one in regular Dutch classes, performed the paradigm in this study
key_sources: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3

article_title: Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students
citation: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. http://eprints.qut.edu.au/
title: The GLIM test: a 36-item instrument for assessing decoding of six graphical languages
description: The Graphical Languages in Mathematics (GLIM) test is a "36-item test" developed to determine students' decoding performance for each of the six graphical languages (Mackinlay, 1999). Items were selected from a bank of 58 items trialled with primary-aged children, drawn from state, national and international year-level mathematics and science tests, with high-literacy-demand items removed. In its final form it comprised six items from each language category, organised into Easy, Moderate and Difficult subtests of 12 items each, scored 0 or 1 per item with a maximum of 12 per difficulty category.
requirements: Items must vary in complexity, require substantial levels of graphical interpretation, and conform to reliability and validity measures
constraints: The instrument was developed for students in the final three years of primary school (Grades 4-6, ages 9-12)
target_learning_goals: decoding graphical languages in mathematics, including number lines, graphs, maps and diagrams
examples: Administered to 317 students approximately 12 months apart in Grades 4, 5 and 6 in approximately 50 minutes within intact classes of 24-31 participants
key_sources: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2009.11.005

article_title: Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions
citation: Olivier, E., Galand, B., Morin, A., & Hospel, V. (2021). Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101389. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101389
title: Global need-supportive teaching configuration: engagement depends on the global level across autonomy support, structure, and involvement
description: This framework holds that classroom engagement is best supported not by each need-supportive practice separately (additive) nor by their combination at high levels (synergistic), but by the overall level a teacher provides across autonomy support, structure, and involvement, "captured by a global factor". The study tested this against two rival configurations using multilevel analyses and found the global account optimal, with imbalance factors playing a secondary role.
requirements: Teachers must provide measurable levels of autonomy support, structure, and involvement that can be modeled as a global factor across practices
constraints: Evidence comes from 8th grade math classrooms in Belgium; the global factor was supported over additive and synergistic alternatives in this setting
target_learners: 8th grade students in secondary mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in the classroom
examples: Multilevel analyses among 1,193 8th grade Belgian students nested in 57 math classrooms contrasted the three configurations of teacher need-supporting practices.
key_sources: Olivier, E., Galand, B., Morin, A., & Hospel, V. (2021). Need-supportive teaching and student engagement in the classroom: Comparing the additive, synergistic, and global contributions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101389. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101389

article_title: Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity
citation: Behnam Karami & Caspar M. Schwiedrzik. (2024). Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00226-w
title: Global pooling strategy for conjunction learning: pure color, pure orientation, and mixed selectivity neurons are jointly read out, enabled by global feedback
description: The article proposes that conjunction learning is best explained by a global pooling readout in which "pure color, pure orientation, and mixed selectivity neurons are combined to give rise to choice information", rather than precision pooling of only the most diagnostic neurons. Global (conjunction-level) feedback permits consistent credit assignment to mixed selectivity representations, whereas feature-specific feedback leaves their credit ambiguous. The framework distinguishes three neuronal resources and two pooling regimes, and predicts faster learning and non-linear task transfer when all resources are engaged.
requirements: Feedback must be delivered at the conjunction level so that credit can be consistently assigned to mixed selectivity representations
constraints: The benefit of global feedback was demonstrated for a linearly separable conjunction task; mixed selectivity was not strictly required to solve the task
The readout-versus-encoding question (whether learning changes encoding or downstream readout) was not resolved in this behavioral study
target_learners: adult human subjects learning visual feature conjunctions
target_learning_goals: discrimination of conjunctive visual features (orientation and color)
examples: Experiment 1 trained subjects with conjunction-level feedback and produced faster learning, larger non-linear mixing, and an XOR transfer advantage relative to feature-specific feedback
key_sources: Behnam Karami & Caspar M. Schwiedrzik. (2024). Visual perceptual learning of feature conjunctions leverages non-linear mixed selectivity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00226-w

article_title: Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data
citation: Rosenheck, Louisa; Cheng, Meng-Tzu; Lin, Chen-Yen; Klopfer, Eric. (2021). Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data. Springer US. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09989-0
title: Game Learning Analytics guiding questions for illuminating content-specific gameplay decisions
description: The article proposes that its three approaches — looking at "actions and tool use, play patterns and player types, and tool input patterns" — could ground "a set of more generalized guiding questions in the GLA field that could be adopted by learning games designers and data scientists". The framework organizes analytics around identifying content-specific gameplay decisions, i.e. methods of completing game tasks related to a domain, so that designers and data scientists can convey information about how students think within a game's subject matter.
requirements: Rich log data granular enough to examine the specific choices most relevant to the context and domain
A game context open-ended enough for students to make choices that demonstrate their thinking
constraints: Developed and illustrated in the context of one selected game quest in a genetics domain
target_learning_goals: Mendelian genetics inquiry and problem solving within a learning game
examples: The study analyzed student exploration of high school level Mendelian genetics in The Radix Endeavor using the three approaches
key_sources: Rosenheck, Louisa; Cheng, Meng-Tzu; Lin, Chen-Yen; Klopfer, Eric. (2021). Approaches to illuminate content-specific gameplay decisions using open-ended game data. Springer US. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09989-0

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Global rating scales for procedural skills assessment
description: Global rating scales are the second method of procedural skills assessment found in current pre-registration practice, with two of the identified tools taking this form. They assess broader examiner abilities with regard to safety and professionalism, report IRR of 0.85 and construct validity with surgical skills abilities, and can be used with certainty in high stakes certification exams, but require expert examiners to assess candidates.
requirements: Need expert examiners to assess candidates
constraints: Cost – need expert examiners to assess candidates
target_learners: medical students assessed by expert practitioners
target_learning_goals: assessment of procedural competence including professionalism and safety
examples: McKinley's generic procedural skills global tool with 4 themes and 42 items, 12 of them procedural, reporting a κ of 0.79 and predicted reliability of 0.79
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Technology-Supported Global Education: A Mixed Method Study = Teknoloji destekli küresel egitim: Bir karma yöntem çalismasi
citation: Egüz, Ş., Öztürk, C. & Kesten, A. (2019). Technology-supported global education: A mixed method study. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(4), 1209-1244. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.040
title: Researcher-developed academic achievement test for the global-education unit
description: A researcher-developed academic achievement test used as the quantitative data collection tool for pre-test, post-test and retention measurement. The article reports it was "a total of 52 questions" reduced to 35 after expert review, then item analysis eliminated 10 questions with discrimination below .30, leaving "a total of 25 multiple choice questions with four options" at moderate difficulty and high discrimination. Reliability was calculated as α=.82 after pre-application with 350 students in four Samsun secondary schools.
requirements: Expert review for validity
Item discrimination of at least .30 for retained items
constraints: Covers only the 'Our country and the world' unit attainments
target_learning_goals: Global-education attainments in the social studies curriculum
examples: Pre-applied to 350 students in four secondary schools in Samsun province before the main application
key_sources: Egüz, Ş., Öztürk, C. & Kesten, A. (2019). Technology-supported global education: A mixed method study. Pegem Eğitim ve Öğretim Dergisi, 9(4), 1209-1244. http://dx.doi.org/10.14527/pegegog.2019.040

article_title: The Impact of Project GLAD on Students' Literacy and Science Learning: Year 1 Results from a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Sheltered Instruction
citation: Theresa Deussen, Elizabeth Autio, Angela Roccograndi, Makoto Hanita. (2014). The Impact of Project GLAD on Students' Literacy and Science Learning: Year 1 Results from a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Sheltered Instruction. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Project GLAD seven-day professional development sequence with demonstration and coaching
description: The professional development element begins with "a two-day workshop, which provides an overview of the approach and an introduction to the instructional strategies." A month or two later, teachers attend a five-day demonstration in which a trainer teaches a compressed unit in a participating teacher's classroom each morning while other teachers observe and a second trainer explains the strategies; afternoons are spent planning teachers' own units with the trainers. Coaching amount is not standardized; study teachers received three days spread over the year.
requirements: Follow-up coaching; in this study three days of coaching spread over the school year
constraints: In this study training was delivered only to fifth-grade teachers, whereas typically all teachers in a school would be trained at the same time
target_learning_goals: Implementing Project GLAD sheltered instruction strategies
examples: All 42 treatment teachers attended all seven days of the training; only five percent of control classrooms showed any GLAD-like strategy in use
key_sources: Theresa Deussen, Elizabeth Autio, Angela Roccograndi, Makoto Hanita. (2014). The Impact of Project GLAD on Students' Literacy and Science Learning: Year 1 Results from a Cluster-Randomized Trial of Sheltered Instruction. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Effect of Glogster and Cooperative Learning Differentiated Instruction on Teachers' Perceptions
citation: Ghada M. Awada and Kawthar H. Faour. (2016). Effect of Glogster and Cooperative Learning Differentiated Instruction on Teachers' Perceptions. Teaching English with Technology, 18(2), 93-114. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: Glogster as a Web 2.0 interactive poster tool for differentiated projects
description: Glogster is a Web 2.0 tool used to create a glog, "an interactive platform in which users create an onlin e poster containing text, video, images, and graphics". The article states it "can be used easily by students of differe nt ages and learning profiles" and that it has 16 key features providing diverse ways of collaboration. In the study, students in groups of four or five created online interactive posters of assigned Science or English topics, embedding Windows Live Movie Maker videos, text, audio, and images, with product forms including PowerPoint, reports, and research findings.
requirements: Teachers received three training workshops covering the Glogster model, cooperative learning, and differentiated instruction before implementation
constraints: The article notes the Lebanese curriculum and national textbooks include no mention of differentiated instruction, so the model was introduced to bridge that disparity
target_learners: Grade 8 EFL and Science learners in public schools
target_learning_goals: Conducting and presenting inquiry projects; research and oral presentation skills
examples: Figures 1-6 show sample Language Arts, Health and Fitness, and Science glogs, Glogpedia searches, uploaded videos, and graphics used by students
key_sources: Ghada M. Awada and Kawthar H. Faour. (2016). Effect of Glogster and Cooperative Learning Differentiated Instruction on Teachers' Perceptions. Teaching English with Technology, 18(2), 93-114. http://www.tewtjournal.org

article_title: Improving English Learners' Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality
citation: Snoder, P. (2017). Improving English Learners’ Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality. TESL Canada Journal, 34(3). https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1277
title: Ask learners to study target collocations in a glossed list for an announced posttest
description: The study's central pedagogical implication is that instructors should induce intentional learning conditions: "asking learners to study target items in a glossed list for an immediate posttest had a powerful effect on their ability to reproduce their form". The authors argue this simple procedure outperformed written tasks and spacing manipulations, and that rote learning from decontextualized glossed lists should be re-evaluated because it is "effective, efficient, and practical".
requirements: Learners must be forewarned of the posttest and instructed to study all target items
constraints: Effect demonstrated for productive form recall in L1-L2 translation testing with adolescent L1 Swedish learners
target_learning_goals: productive knowledge of verb-noun collocation form
examples: In Treatment 3, participants studied a glossed list of 14 target collocations for an announced test after 15 minutes
key_sources: Snoder, P. (2017). Improving English Learners’ Productive Collocation Knowledge: The Effects of Involvement Load, Spacing, and Intentionality. TESL Canada Journal, 34(3). https://doi.org/10.18806/tesl.v34i3.1277

article_title: Screening efficiency over experience: Rapid target detection in low-power field as a modifiable cognitive biomarker for diagnostic accuracy in digital cytology.
citation: Abe, N., Nishimura, Y., Yamashita, K., Kawamorita, T., Takatori, Y., Murakumo, Y., & Furuta, R. (2026). Screening efficiency over experience: Rapid target detection in low-power field as a modifiable cognitive biomarker for diagnostic accuracy in digital cytology. Cancer Cytopathology. https://doi.org/10.1002/cncy.70132
title: Global-focal search model of visual expertise in medical image perception
description: The article invokes the "global‐focal search model" from medical image perception research to explain why LPF efficiency predicts accuracy. Expert practitioners "employ a holistic processing strategy that leverages parafoveal vision to rapidly extract global information from the entire scene", allowing abnormalities to "pop out" before attention is given to them. This explains why high-accuracy cytotechnologists showed shorter LPF fixation times, whereas low performers' prolonged LPF duration reflects inefficient serial processing of irrelevant background features.
requirements: Consolidated search images acquired through experience or structured training that enable rapid global extraction of scene information.
constraints: The article notes low performers' prolonged fixations reflect a serial processing strategy in which attention is inefficiently deployed to irrelevant background features.
target_learning_goals: Visual diagnostic expertise
Rapid target detection
Selective visual attention
examples: A representative high performer completed the task in 14 seconds with a rhythmic LPF-to-HPF progression, while a low performer took 104 seconds with fragmented, recursive scanning.
key_sources: Abe, N., Nishimura, Y., Yamashita, K., Kawamorita, T., Takatori, Y., Murakumo, Y., & Furuta, R. (2026). Screening efficiency over experience: Rapid target detection in low-power field as a modifiable cognitive biomarker for diagnostic accuracy in digital cytology. Cancer Cytopathology. https://doi.org/10.1002/cncy.70132

article_title: Global trends and practice patterns in virtual reality simulation training for ophthalmic surgery: an international survey use of virtual reality simulation training around the world.
citation: Dormegny Lea, Yaïci Remi, Koestel Emilia, Dhubhghaill Sorcha Ní, Ahiwalay Chetan, Bacchav Ashish, Bourges Jean-Louis, Dechriste Gauthier, Dick H. Burkhard, Filipe Helena Prior, Flockerzi Elias, Gaucher David, Lansingh Van Charles, Gonzalez Pamela, Henderson Bonnie An, Kuntz Salome, Rafanomezantsoa Rindra, Andre Jean-Marie, Rocha Guillermo, Rousseau Antoine, Sauer Arnaud, Schaeffer Marion, Seitz Berthold, Solecki Lauriana, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Chakfe Nabil, Lejay Anne, Bourcier Tristan. (2025). Global trends and practice patterns in virtual reality simulation training for ophthalmic surgery: an international survey use of virtual reality simulation training around the world. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-16227-7
title: 39-question Global Practice Patterns of Virtual Reality Simulation Training survey
description: An anonymous 39-question survey entitled "Global Practice Patterns of Virtual Reality Simulation Training", created on SurveyMonkey and reviewed for relevance by ophthalmologists with VRS expertise. It was emailed on November 20th, 2023 to first or last authors of ophthalmology VRS publications on Pubmed and to directors of centers using VRS, with two follow-up reminders, closing March 31st, 2024. Respondents reported gender, age, position, simulator access, training time, module completion, and opinions on a surgical license.
requirements: Consent for academic, aggregated, anonymous use of answers was obtained via the final survey question.
constraints: The response rate was 11%, with low representation from the UK, Ireland, Turkey, Morocco, Egypt, Argentina, Brazil, Hong Kong and China.
target_learning_goals: characterizing global virtual reality simulation training practice patterns in ophthalmic surgical education
examples: 1845 questionnaires were distributed across 36 countries; 170 responses from 26 countries were analyzed after removing 29 questionnaires.

article_title: Evaluation of glasses-free 3D anatomy learning materials through a randomized control study with a puzzle-like method.
citation: Muro S, Miyosawa K, Yamaguchi K, Okamoto K, Okamoto S, Itamiya T, Akita K. (2025). Evaluation of glasses‐free 3D anatomy learning materials through a randomized control study with a puzzle‐like method. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70063
title: Glasses-free 3D anatomy learning materials for abdominal organs and blood vessels compatible with the Sony EFL-SR1 display
description: This element is a set of 3D anatomy learning materials built in Unity from the Visible Korean Human segmented data, covering abdominal organs and blood vessels, and designed for the autostereoscopic Sony EFL-SR1 tabletop display. It "provides features essential for learning (e.g., structure labeling, rotation, zoom in/out, the possibility of moving the 3D objects, toggling the visibility of each organ, and changing the transparency of each organ)". In the study it served as the identical learning content shown to both display groups.
requirements: A compatible glasses-free 3D spatial reality tabletop display and controller; operation was simplified to horizontal rotation only to reduce burden on participants.
constraints: Effectiveness was evaluated only for abdominal organs and blood vessels, with a three-minute learning session in a single-university sample.
target_learning_goals: Understanding the spatial arrangement of abdominal anatomical structures
examples: In the RCT, the 2D group viewed the same material via the EFL-SR1's 2D display function while the 3D group viewed it in glasses-free 3D.
key_sources: Muro S, Miyosawa K, Yamaguchi K, Okamoto K, Okamoto S, Itamiya T, Akita K. (2025). Evaluation of glasses‐free 3D anatomy learning materials through a randomized control study with a puzzle‐like method. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70063

article_title: The Impact of Simulation-Based Trabeculectomy Training on Resident Core Surgical Skill Competency.
citation: Annoh R, Buchan J, Gichuhi S, et al. (2023). The impact of simulation-based trabeculectomy training on resident core surgical skill competency. Journal of Glaucoma. https://doi.org/10.1097/IJG.0000000000002114
title: GLASS one-week trabeculectomy simulation course with Sim-OSSCAR competency assessment
description: The GLASS intervention is a one-week intensive trabeculectomy simulation-based surgical education course combining theoretical and practical teaching. "The surgical procedure was deconstructed and instruction in surgical steps was provided using a modified Peyton's four-stage approach", with low-cost moderate-fidelity materials (foam for suturing, apple peels for scleral flaps) and full procedures on high-fidelity synthetic Advanced TrabEye eyes under Zeiss microscopes. Competency was assessed with the validated Sim-OSSCAR rubric by two independent, masked expert graders scoring eight core skills to a maximum of 16 per video.
requirements: Requires high-fidelity synthetic simulation eyes, operating microscopes, video recording equipment, and graders trained in the Sim-OSSCAR rubric
constraints: The article states results only apply to simulated surgical skill competency using high-fidelity artificial eyes, and live surgical skills could not be evaluated due to low trabeculectomy case numbers
target_learners: resident ophthalmologists in postgraduate training years two to four
target_learning_goals: competency in the eight core trabeculectomy surgical skills including scleral incision, scleral flap, releasable suturing, conjunctival suturing and sclerostomy
examples: Procedures on the Advanced TrabEye eyes were recorded with the Zeiss Labscope App on iPads and graded by two masked expert graders, each video allocated a random seven-digit number
key_sources: Annoh R, Buchan J, Gichuhi S, et al. (2023). The impact of simulation-based trabeculectomy training on resident core surgical skill competency. Journal of Glaucoma. https://doi.org/10.1097/IJG.0000000000002114
